name: CV / Resume Analysis - Backend Developer
description: Signals extracted from the user's CV/resume to evidence Backend Developer skills. CV data provides self-reported information that must be cross-validated with GitHub and assessment sources.

extraction_rules.description: How to extract and weight information from CV content for Backend roles.

sections.description: Explicit list of technologies, languages, and databases mentioned in skills section.
sections.notes: Low strength because listing a technology doesn't prove proficiency. Listing 'PostgreSQL' or 'Kafka' alone is insufficient without concrete project or work experience.

sections.description: Job descriptions and responsibilities mentioning backend engineering activities.
sections.notes: Higher strength when specific actions, architectural decisions, and quantifiable throughput/latency outcomes are described.
quality_indicators: Specific technologies, databases, and message brokers mentioned in architectural context (e.g. 'designed Kafka event-driven pipeline handling 50k RPS')
Quantifiable outcomes (reduced p99 latency from 450ms to 40ms, scaled database read throughput by 5x using read replicas)
Action verbs indicating hands-on backend engineering (architected, migrated, optimized, scaled, decomposed, hardened)
Duration, scale, and recency of backend systems experience

sections.description: Personal or open-source backend projects demonstrating architectural depth.
sections.notes: Higher strength if linked to GitHub repository with clean test suites, migrations, and docker-compose setups.
quality_indicators: Technical depth of project description (e.g. 'built an idempotent payment processing service with outbox pattern and distributed locks')
Architectural patterns used match claimed competencies (DDD, Hexagonal, CQRS)
Links to live API documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI) or source code
Complexity indicators (distributed transactions, caching layers, OpenTelemetry tracing)

sections.description: Relevant computer science, software engineering, or technical degrees.
sections.notes: Provides foundation in data structures, algorithms, and database theory, but does not substitute practical backend systems experience.

sections.description: Professional certifications relevant to backend and database engineering.
sections.notes: Certifications indicate theoretical domain knowledge and should be cross-validated with code and assessments.

cloud_architecture: AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate / Professional
database_data: Confluent Certified Developer for Apache Kafka (CCDAK)

signal_mapping.description: How CV mentions map to skill evidence using COMPOSITE KEYS ({skill_id}.{subskill_id}). AI should use these patterns.

patterns.pattern: Describes designing relational database schemas and optimizing complex SQL queries
Lists PostgreSQL, MySQL, or MongoDB in skills list only
Describes designing and building RESTful or GraphQL APIs with OpenAPI contracts
Architected event-driven microservices using Apache Kafka or RabbitMQ
Implemented Clean Architecture, Hexagonal Architecture, or Domain-Driven Design (DDD)
Implemented OAuth2, OpenID Connect, JWT, or RBAC authorization systems
Implemented distributed caching with Redis and eliminated cache stampedes
Wrote comprehensive unit and integration tests using Testcontainers or Pact
Engineered fault tolerance with Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads, and retry policies
Instrumented application observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, and structured logging
Architected CQRS and Event Sourcing data pipelines
Has AWS Solutions Architect or Confluent Kafka certification without project evidence

important_notes: CV data is self-reported and inherently unreliable as standalone evidence
Always cross-validate CV claims with GitHub code and adaptive assessment results
Backend certifications indicate theoretical knowledge but do not prove hands-on systems reliability skills
Look for quantifiable systems metrics — 'reduced p99 query latency by 80%' is stronger than 'optimized database'
Look for architectural intentionality: trade-off justifications (e.g. why Kafka was chosen over RabbitMQ)
Recency and scale matter — managing a microservice handling 50k RPS differs fundamentally from a low-traffic internal CRUD API
